title: Prerequisites: Everything You Need Before Lesson 1
summary: The knowledge the OSDev community expects before you write a kernel: numbers and memory, C for systems work, assembly, how code becomes a program, and a working toolbox. Take only the modules you need.
goal: Read hex and memory layouts fluently, write C that is safe next to hardware, read and write basic x86 assembly, explain what the compiler and linker produce, and drive GCC, Make, Git, QEMU and GDB from a Unix-like shell.

modules.title: Start here
modules.summary: What the community expects you to know, how to tell where you stand, and how to learn and ask well.

lessons.title: What you need to know before writing a kernel
lessons.why: Kernel work assumes skills no tutorial teaches along the way. Knowing the list up front tells you which modules here you can skip and which you must not.
objectives: List the skill areas the OSDev community expects before kernel work.
Mark each area as solid, shaky or missing for yourself.
lessons.checkpoint: Write down the skill areas from the reading and rate yourself on each: solid, shaky or missing. Every shaky or missing area maps to a module in this section; that is your study plan.

lessons.title: The computer science underneath
lessons.why: Everything later rests on how digital circuits represent and move bits. A clear picture of logic, circuits and abstraction layers makes hardware chapters readable instead of magical.
objectives: Explain how layers of abstraction manage the complexity of an electronic system.
Describe what logic gates do with bits.
lessons.checkpoint: In your own words, explain the layers between a logic gate and a running program, and name one layer an OS developer has to reach below that an application developer never sees.

lessons.title: Learning well and asking for help
lessons.why: You will get stuck, and the OSDev community is your best help. A well-asked question gets an answer; a vague one gets ignored. Writing it well often solves the problem before you post.
objectives: Write a question that states your goal, what you tried and the exact failure.
Know what research to do before asking.
lessons.checkpoint: Take a bug you hit recently (any project) and write it up as a forum question following the reading: goal, environment, minimal code, exact output, what you already tried.

modules.title: Numbers, bits and memory
modules.summary: How values look to the hardware: binary and hex, byte order, real numbers, and where a program's data lives.

lessons.title: Binary and hexadecimal by hand
lessons.why: Addresses, flags and device registers are written in hex and read as bits. Converting by hand, and masking out fields, is a daily kernel skill.
objectives: Convert byte- and word-sized values between binary, hex and decimal without a calculator.
Extract and set bit fields with AND, OR and shifts.
lessons.checkpoint: By hand: write 0x2F in binary and decimal, write 200 in hex, then compute (0x00403007 >> 12) & 0x3FF and explain each step.

lessons.title: Byte order: endianness
lessons.why: x86 stores multi-byte values backwards from how you write them. Disk formats and network packets often use the other order. Endianness bugs look like random corruption until you know to look.
objectives: Predict the byte layout of a 32-bit value on a little-endian CPU.
Say when a value must be byte-swapped.
lessons.checkpoint: Write 0xDEADBEEF as the four bytes a little-endian memory dump shows, then as the bytes a big-endian network packet carries.

lessons.title: Real numbers in a computer
lessons.why: Floating point has its own registers and its own state that a kernel must save on every task switch. Knowing the format explains why kernels often avoid floats entirely.
objectives: Split an IEEE 754 single into sign, exponent and mantissa.
Explain why 0.1 cannot be stored exactly.
lessons.checkpoint: Decode the 32-bit float 0x40490FDB by hand into sign, exponent and mantissa, and say roughly what value it is.

lessons.title: Where a program's data lives
lessons.why: Your kernel has to provide every one of these regions itself: read-only data, globals, the stack and the heap. Knowing what each is for comes before building them.
objectives: Name the memory regions of a running program and what lives in each.
Explain how the stack grows and what a stack frame holds.
lessons.checkpoint: For a small C program with a string literal, a global, a local array and a malloc call, say which region each lives in and in which direction the stack and heap grow.

modules.title: C for systems programmers
modules.summary: The C you need next to hardware: the language's sharp edges, the preprocessor, volatile and memory-mapped registers, headers and the C library, undefined behaviour.

lessons.title: C, the language of kernels
lessons.why: Almost every hobby kernel and every tutorial on the wiki is written in C. Pointers, pointer arithmetic and manual memory are the tools you will use on every page.
objectives: Explain what a pointer holds and what dereferencing and pointer arithmetic do.
Say why C suits kernel work.
lessons.checkpoint: Write a C function that takes a uint8_t* and a length and prints a hex dump of that memory, 16 bytes per line with the address on the left. Run it on a local array.

lessons.title: The C preprocessor
lessons.why: Kernels use macros for constants, register layouts and per-architecture code. Knowing that the preprocessor is plain text substitution, run before the compiler, saves hours of confusion.
objectives: Trace what #include, #define and #ifdef produce.
Spot the classic macro pitfalls.
lessons.checkpoint: Write a header with an include guard, a constant, a function-like macro and an #ifdef block. Run gcc -E on a file that uses it and explain the output.

lessons.title: Talking to hardware from C: volatile and memory-mapped registers
lessons.why: The optimiser assumes memory only changes when your code writes it. Device registers break that rule. Without volatile your driver works at -O0 and silently fails at -O2.
objectives: Explain what volatile tells the compiler and what it does not guarantee.
Declare a memory-mapped register correctly in C.
lessons.checkpoint: Write a loop that polls a status register until a bit is set, once with volatile and once without. Compile both with gcc -O2 -S and point to the difference in the assembly.

lessons.title: Headers, declarations and the C library
articles: Why function implementations shouldn't be put in header files
lessons.why: A kernel has no C library until you write one. Knowing what belongs in a header, and which libc parts are compiler-provided versus OS-provided, decides what your kernel can use on day one.
objectives: Separate declarations from definitions across headers and source files.
Say which headers a freestanding compiler still provides.
lessons.checkpoint: Split a small program into main.c, util.c and util.h with no definitions in the header. Then list which standard headers remain available with -ffreestanding.

lessons.title: Undefined behaviour
lessons.why: Undefined behaviour lets the compiler assume things that are false in a kernel, then delete your code. A sanitiser finds it for you, if you know to switch it on.
objectives: Name common sources of undefined behaviour in C.
Explain what UBSan reports and how a kernel hooks it.
lessons.checkpoint: Write a program with a signed overflow and an out-of-bounds shift, build it with -fsanitize=undefined on your host and read the reports.

modules.title: Assembly
modules.summary: Enough x86 assembly to read your compiler's output and write the parts C cannot: registers, syntax, assemblers and the boundary between C and assembly.

lessons.title: What assembly is
lessons.why: Boot code, interrupt entry and context switches must be written in assembly, and reading disassembly is how you debug everything else.
objectives: Explain the relationship between assembly, machine code and an ISA.
Say which parts of a kernel need assembly.
lessons.checkpoint: Compile int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } with gcc -O2 -S -m32 and explain every line of the output.

lessons.title: The x86 registers
lessons.why: General registers, segment registers, flags and control registers all appear in kernel code. CR0 and CR3 alone switch on protected mode and paging.
objectives: Name the general, segment, flag and control registers and what each is for.
Explain how EAX, AX, AH and AL overlap.
lessons.checkpoint: Without looking: what are EAX, AX, AH and AL after mov eax, 0x12345678? Which register holds the page directory address, and which bit of CR0 enables paging?

lessons.title: Choosing an assembler and its syntax
lessons.why: Wiki code comes in two syntaxes: Intel (NASM) and AT&T (GAS). Mixing them up reverses operands and silently breaks code.
objectives: Read the same instruction in Intel and AT&T syntax.
Assemble a file with NASM and with GAS.
lessons.checkpoint: Write mov eax, [ebx+4] in AT&T syntax, assemble one small file with both nasm and as, and compare the bytes with objdump -d.

lessons.title: Learning x86 assembly
lessons.why: Your first boot code runs in 16-bit real mode. Writing a few small real-mode programs builds the instinct you need for lesson 1.2.3.
objectives: Write a loop, a comparison and a function call in x86 assembly.
Print text from real mode using a BIOS call.
lessons.checkpoint: Write a 16-bit routine that prints a null-terminated string with the BIOS teletype call, and step through it once in a debugger or emulator.

lessons.title: Mixing C and assembly
lessons.why: Port I/O, reading control registers and halting the CPU need assembly inside C. Get the constraints or the calling convention wrong and the compiler quietly breaks your code.
objectives: Write inline assembly with correct input, output and clobber constraints.
Call an assembly function from C under the cdecl convention.
lessons.checkpoint: Write inline-assembly wrappers outb(port, value) and inb(port), and an assembly function that C calls as int add3(int, int, int). Check the generated code with objdump.

modules.title: How code becomes a program
modules.summary: What the compiler, assembler and linker each produce, the ELF format, and how kernel, compiler and C library fit together.

lessons.title: Compilers
further: Why do I need a Cross Compiler?
lessons.why: You need to know what the compiler produces, and what it assumes about the target, before you can tell it to produce code for a machine with no OS.
objectives: Name the stages from source file to object file.
Explain what a target triple says.
lessons.checkpoint: Run gcc -save-temps on a small file and identify the .i, .s and .o outputs. Say which stage produced each.

lessons.title: Linkers and object files
lessons.why: Your kernel's memory layout is decided by the linker, through a linker script you write. Symbol resolution and relocation errors are among the first build failures you will meet.
objectives: Explain symbol resolution and relocation.
Read a symbol table with nm.
lessons.checkpoint: Build two object files where one calls a function defined in the other. Run nm on both and on the linked result, and explain U, T and the final addresses.

lessons.title: Executable formats: ELF
lessons.why: GRUB loads your kernel as an ELF file, and later your kernel loads user programs the same way. Sections, segments and the entry point are what both loaders read.
objectives: Distinguish sections from program segments.
Find the entry point and loadable segments with readelf.
lessons.checkpoint: Run readelf -h -l -S on any ELF binary and point out the entry point, each PT_LOAD segment's address and size, and which sections fall inside it.

lessons.title: Kernel, compiler and C library together
articles: How kernel, compiler, and C library work together
further: Why do I need a Cross Compiler?
lessons.why: This is the map of who provides what: the compiler's own runtime, the C library and the system calls under it. Your kernel replaces the bottom of that stack.
objectives: Say which layer provides printf, memcpy, system calls and libgcc helpers.
Explain what changes when there is no OS underneath.
lessons.checkpoint: Draw the stack from your program down to the hardware: application, C library, system calls, kernel. Mark which parts your kernel must provide itself.

modules.title: Your workbench
modules.summary: The tools every lesson assumes: a Unix-like shell, GCC and binutils, Make, Git, an emulator and a debugger.

lessons.title: A Unix-like environment, on any OS
lessons.why: The OSDev toolchain and tutorials assume a Unix-like shell. On Windows, WSL gives you one; on Linux and macOS you already have it.
objectives: Get a working shell with gcc, make and git.
Move files between the host and the Unix environment.
lessons.checkpoint: In your Unix-like shell, run gcc --version, make --version, git --version and qemu-system-i386 --version, and install whatever is missing.

lessons.title: GCC and binutils
lessons.why: GCC and binutils (as, ld, objdump, readelf, nm, objcopy) are the tools you will run thousands of times. Knowing their key flags makes every later lesson faster.
objectives: Compile, assemble and link separately with gcc, as and ld.
Inspect binaries with objdump, readelf and nm.
lessons.checkpoint: Build a two-file program in separate steps (gcc -c, then ld or gcc to link), then disassemble one function with objdump -d.

lessons.title: Build automation with Make
lessons.why: A kernel quickly grows to dozens of files, assembly and C mixed. Make rebuilds only what changed and turns build, run and debug into one command each.
objectives: Write rules with targets, prerequisites and recipes.
Use pattern rules and automatic variables.
lessons.checkpoint: Write a Makefile for a three-file C project with a pattern rule for .o files, a clean target and a run target. Touch one file and confirm only it is rebuilt.

lessons.title: Version control with Git
lessons.why: You will break your kernel daily. Committing every working state means you can always get back to the last kernel that booted, and see exactly what changed.
objectives: Commit, inspect history and go back to an earlier state.
Use a branch for an experiment.
lessons.checkpoint: Put a project in Git, make three commits, break something on a branch, then use git diff and git log to find the change and return to the working version.

lessons.title: Emulators: QEMU and Bochs
lessons.why: You will boot your kernel hundreds of times a day. An emulator does it in a second, cannot be bricked, and lets you inspect the machine when things go wrong.
objectives: Boot an image in QEMU with serial output to the terminal.
Pick between QEMU and Bochs for a given job.
lessons.checkpoint: Boot any small disk image or ISO in qemu-system-i386 with -serial stdio, open the QEMU monitor and run info registers.

lessons.title: Debugging with GDB
further: QEMU and GDB in long mode
lessons.why: When the screen stays black, GDB attached to QEMU shows exactly where the CPU is and what the registers hold. It replaces guessing with looking.
objectives: Set breakpoints, step and inspect registers and memory in GDB.
Attach GDB to QEMU's gdbstub.
lessons.checkpoint: Debug a host C program in GDB: break in a function, step, print a variable, and examine memory with x/16xb. Then start QEMU with -s -S and connect with target remote :1234.
